messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 68

He is 63, broad-shouldered and weathered from decades in construction, a man who still measures time by shifts, weather, and what a body can carry. He grew up in Oceania and came of age believing that endurance is a kind of love: you work hard, you keep your word, you do not complain. By the time he meets with the therapist, he is widowed and lives alone. He speaks in a steady, practical way at first, but the story of what happened with his later partner comes out slowly, as if each piece has to be pried loose.

He meets her several years after his wife dies. In the beginning, he experiences the relationship as a relief from loneliness. She is lively, attentive, and seems to understand the emptiness that settled over him after bereavement. He has spent most of his life on building sites, where the rules are visible and tasks have an order: pour the slab, set the frame, finish the roof. At home with her, the rules begin shifting in ways he cannot name. She becomes sharp with him over small things—how long he stays at work, who he talks to, where he leaves his boots. He tells himself she is stressed. He has worked with volatile foremen before; he knows how to keep his head down and wait for a storm to pass.

The first time she hits him, they are in the kitchen. He is late getting home after a concrete pour runs over. She accuses him of lying, of choosing work over her, and before he fully understands what is happening, she throws a mug that catches his shoulder and then strikes him across the face. What lodges in his mind afterward is not only the pain but the disbelief. He is a strong man, taller and heavier than she is, and he feels ashamed that he stands there stunned, saying nothing. The next morning he goes to work with a split lip and tells the crew he walked into a cupboard door. He says it with a laugh, hating himself while he says it.

After that, the violence becomes part of the landscape of his life. She shoves him in hallways, scratches his arms, throws tools and plates, corners him in rooms and dares him to defend himself so she can call him the aggressor. He becomes hyperaware of the sound of her footsteps and the set of her jaw. He starts parking outside the house in a way that lets him leave quickly. He keeps his phone hidden and his keys in the same pocket at all times. At work, where he once takes pride in being reliable and calm, he finds himself flinching when metal drops or someone shouts across the site. The bang of a nail gun can send a shock through his chest. He becomes distracted on scaffolding, looking down too quickly when he hears raised voices below, his heart pounding as though danger is right behind him.

He does not tell anyone. Part of him cannot make his story fit with the kind of man he has always believed himself to be. Part of him fears no one will believe him. When a coworker jokes that he has gone quiet since “finding himself a fiery one,” he smiles tightly and changes the subject. At night he sleeps lightly, if at all. He lies listening for movement in the house, every creak pulling him awake. When he does sleep, he dreams in fragments: being trapped in a narrow corridor, bracing for impact, trying to shout and finding no voice. He wakes sweaty and disoriented, sometimes already out of bed before he fully comes to.

Eventually the relationship ends after a particularly violent night when she strikes him repeatedly with a lamp and he locks himself in the bathroom until dawn. Even after she is gone, his body behaves as if she could return at any moment. He checks the windows before bed, then checks them again. If a car slows outside his house, he freezes and listens. He avoids the street where they used to shop and takes the long way to jobs to avoid passing her neighborhood. He keeps busy because stillness is dangerous; on weekends he repairs fences that do not need repairing and reorganizes his shed for the third or fourth time. Yet concentration slips away from him. He rereads work orders, forgets measurements he has just taken, and grows angry with himself for mistakes he never used to make.

Being widowed had already taught him what it means to live with absence, but this is different. Grief had felt heavy and sad; this feels like occupation. He says he no longer recognizes himself. He startles at touch. He sits in cafés facing the door. He mistrusts friendliness, scans strangers’ expressions for signs of mockery or threat, and keeps conversations shallow. Shame trails him everywhere. He feels humiliated that he “let it happen,” then immediately feels unfair for using that phrase, as if he should have controlled something that was never his to control.

Now, in the therapist’s office, he speaks about the abuse in pieces, often staring at his hands. He notices the room’s exits without meaning to. Sometimes, while recounting a memory, he falls silent and seems to be listening to another place entirely. He says he is tired of living as though the attack is always about to happen again. He wants one full night of sleep. He wants to walk onto a job site and hear ordinary noise as ordinary noise. Most of all, he wants to feel that his life belongs in the present, instead of remaining trapped in those rooms where he learned to watch, wait, and brace.
